newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - American General sees savings.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - American General sees savings.

text.p: American General Corp expects to achieve cost savings of about $50 million through layoffs and consolidation of operations in its proposed $1.8 billion acquisition of USLIFE Corp, Chief Executive Robert Devlin said Thursday.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, Devlin said it was not yet clear how many positions would be eliminated as a result of the merger.
He said he expects the deal to become additive to earnings by the third quarter of 1998, presuming it closes as planned by the second quarter of 1997.
The deal, announced earlier today, is not expected to dilute earnings in 1997, he said.
Devlin said USLIFE will become a wholly-owned subsidiary of American General.

He said he would continue as chief executive of American General and, as previously planned, would take on the additional post of chairman when the current chairman, Harold Hook, retires later this year.
American General's headquarters will remain in Houston, but the company plans to use some of USLIFE's New York offices as well, Devlin said.
He said American General will likely consolidate its New York operation into USLIFE's much larger New York franchise.
In addition, he said, he expects to merge the two companies' credit life insurance operations, creating the nation's second largest credit life business.
USLIFE's credit life business is based in Schaumberg, Ill., and American General's is in Evanston, Ind., he said.
Devlin said the top management at USLIFE had not yet been determined. He said he was working with USLIFE Chairman Gordon Crosby on those positions.
Although he expects the deal to be additive to earnings in 1998, Devlin said it was too early to say how much it might contribute.
"Right now it's difficult to speculate on," he said. "We've got a lot of work to do."
The merger will strengthen American General's core businesses and will be a good strategic fit, Devlin said.
"It strengthens our position in our markets," he said, but it does not give American General any new product lines.
"We weren't looking for (new product lines)," Devlin said. "We were looking for something to strengthen and enhance what we currently had."
The deal will give American General a market capitalization of about $10 billion, ranking it fourth among U.S. insurers, he said.
The deal's roots go back a long way, but the actual negotiations took place over the last 10 days, he said.
The talks got off the ground through the assistance of Western National Corp Chairman Michael Poulos.
Poulos worked for USLIFE from 1958 through 1970 and maintained a close relationship with Crosby, the USLIFE chairman, Devlin said.
After leaving USLIFE, Poulos joined American General, where he became president of the company. Poulos left American General and became chairman of Western National in 1993.
Devlin said he worked for Poulos when he first joined American General.
Although Devlin said he had met Crosby several times at industry conferences, he said he asked Poulos to arrange a meeting.
"I had asked Mike if he would get the two of us together and introduce me to Gordon so I would get to know him a little better," Devlin said.

"Gordon and I started talking and he knew we were interested in his firm and I think he was interested in us because he, as I do, felt it was a great strategic fit, an excellent merger, very complementary in many respects," he said.
"About 10 days ago Gordon and I sat down and began our initial conversations and it evolved into this," Devlin said.
USLIFE was advised by Goldman Sachs and the law firm of Debevoise & Plimpton. American General was advised by Merrill Lynch and the law firm of Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom.
